text: This is Elon Musk, the first trillionaire in human history. You probably think his new fight with India is just about a satellite internet license. Back in 2024, security forces in Manipur had seized Starlink equipment alongside weapons, even though Musk says Starlink's beams are switched off over India. The very next day, a young activist named Abhijit Dipke launched a satirical movement called the Cockroach Janta Party. It began as a joke, but it caught the anger of millions of young Indians about jobs, prices, and who really runs the country. The ruling BJP called the protest a flop show, and police said the protest site itself stayed clear. The protesters say they were silenced, the government says it kept order, and the movement has promised to keep going. Now, put the two stories side by side. On one side, a young, angry country with an opposition leader attacking the government over elections and big business, on the other side, a trillionaire with a global megaphone attacking the same government over the same tycoons in the very same week. To be clear, there's no public evidence that Musk has said a word about these protests. But critics in India warn that this is exactly the kind of moment an outsider with a huge platform can use when a country is already divided. One post amplified to hundreds of millions of people can pour fuel on a fire that's already burning. Musk's supporters see it very differently. They say he's a businessman who waited five years and simply set out loud what many Indians already suspect about crony capitalism. So, is he a whistleblower or is he a player? He owns the rockets, the satellites, the social network, and an artificial intelligence company. No private citizen has ever controlled this many of the pipes that information flows through. And for someone who already has everything money can buy, many analysts argue that what's left is influence. Remember the switch over Crimea? Now, imagine that same kind of switch over a country where hundreds of millions of people could one day get their internet from the sky. Not just a delayed license, but a five-year fight over the sky, a tycoon who rewrote India's telecom market, and a trillionaire who has stepped into politics from America to Brazil, Germany, and Britain. And now, in a 10th week for Indian democracy, his posts landed right in the middle of it. Starlink could bring the internet to villages that have waited decades for it.
